rationale: A wins because its third angle, "Replit's Agent Promises Working Apps. It Won't Say How Often They Actually Work," is the sharper reporter bait: it turns the launch's biggest unsupported claim into an accountability story and then admits exactly what proof is missing. B is strong, but "When the AI does the building, Replit charges for the work, not the seat" gets too cute with a pricing fact that is actually usage-based on top of subscriptions. That is a useful business-model lens, but the headline overstates the evidence; A is cleaner and more disciplined.
gaps_in_A: "replaces the development workflow for non-engineers entirely" outruns the update. The facts support app generation, database setup, and deployment, not replacement of the whole development workflow.
"explicitly declines to disclose reliability rates" overstates the silence. The update says reliability is not disclosed; it does not say Replit declined when asked.
"contradicting its own founding premise" is a shade too declarative. The supplied facts say Replit is used heavily in education, not that education was its founding premise.
The pricing refusal is a little too absolute: "There is no rate, no comparison point, no user impact data" is true, but a narrow business-model angle could survive if proof-gated.
gaps_in_B: "charges for the work, not the seat" is too neat and partly wrong. The supplied fact is usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions, not instead of subscriptions.
"whether agents break seat-based pricing" turns one Replit pricing detail into a market-shift claim. That needs more than the company update gives.
"built its name teaching people to code" stretches the evidence. The update says Replit is a browser-based coding platform used heavily in education; it does not prove the whole brand identity.

B buries the cleanest accountability angle as a proof question: "How often do agent-generated apps actually work without fixes?" deserved consideration as its own story, not just homework before pitching.
